chapter_title: Before We Go, Part 2: Traveling Well and the Learning for All Thread
learning_objective: The learner will judge which of three responses best fits the six thoughtful-traveler principles in each of eight situations on our route, choosing the best response in at least 7 of 8 situations on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** thoughtful-traveler-choices
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate
**Bloom Verb:** judge
**Learning Objective:** The learner will judge which of three responses best fits the six thoughtful-traveler principles in each of eight situations on our route, choosing the best response in at least 7 of 8 situations on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** thoughtful traveler, the six principles (curiosity, humility, consent, reciprocity, patience, many stories), tourist script, empathy, cognitive and emotional empathy (all defined in the sections "The Thoughtful Traveler" and "Empathy in Travel" above). **Evidence of Mastery:** For each situation the learner commits to one of three responses. A choice is correct when it matches the Best response column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the principle list is exploration, not evidence; the committed choice is the evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Being polite means avoiding contact (keeping conversations brief, refusing tea). (2) Photographing someone from a distance is harmless because they do not notice. (3) Correcting a local guide with "the real story" is helpful. (4) Off-season limits are poor service rather than a normal part of the season. (5) A kind lie ("I'll come back later") is kinder than an honest no. **Instructional Rationale:** Evaluate-level judgment needs cases where several answers are plausible and the learner must weigh them against stated criteria. Each situation offers one weak, one tempting and one best response, and the feedback names the principle that decides it, so the learner practices applying criteria rather than recalling rules. **Content:** The six principles, shown on screen for reference throughout: Curiosity (ask and look closer); Humility (we are guests); Consent (people and sacred places are not scenery); Reciprocity (fair exchange, no false promises); Patience (fit the place's rhythm); Many stories (listen to more than one account). | # | Situation shown to the learner | Response A | Response B | Response C | Best response | Principle | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | Day 1, Istanbul. A woman selling simit (sesame bread rings) from a red cart would make a perfect photo. | Take a quick photo from across the street so you do not bother her. | Buy a simit, smile, raise the camera with a questioning look, and accept a shake of the head. | Photograph only the cart, but frame her at the edge of the shot. | B | Consent | A person is not scenery; asking, and accepting a no, treats her as someone at work rather than part of the view. | | 2 | Day 3, Istanbul. You reach a mosque just as the call to prayer begins. | Slip in quietly at the back to watch the prayer. | Go in, but keep the camera down. | Wait outside or visit somewhere nearby, and come back after the prayer ends. | C | Consent | During prayer the mosque is doing its first job, worship; visitors return when it reopens to them. | | 3 | Day 6, Gallipoli. The Turkish guide's account of the battle differs from an Australian film you have seen. | Listen, then ask what the battle means to the guide's own family. | Politely point out what the film said. | Tune out, since you already know the story. | A | Many stories | The guide is telling the story as Turks remember it; asking about family turns a script into a conversation. | | 4 | Day 8, Rhodes. In November the taverna's menu is short and the kitchen closes early. | Ask for the full summer menu anyway. | Leave and post a review about the limited menu. | Ask what is good today and what is in season. | C | Patience | Off-season staff and supplies are cut back; asking what is fresh gets the best meal and respects a hard season. | | 5 | Day 4, Istanbul. A carpet seller invites you in for tea, and you know you will not buy. | Accept the tea, enjoy the talk, and say kindly and clearly that you are not buying today. | Refuse firmly, because tea is a sales trick. | Accept, and promise to come back later even though you will not. | A | Reciprocity | Hospitality is real even in trade; an honest no respects his time more than a false promise. | | 6 | Day 11, Athens. The café has no English menu and the waiter speaks little English. | Speak English slowly and loudly. | Say *kaliméra* ("good morning"), then point, smile, or use a phone translation. | Leave for a café with an English menu. | B | Humility | A greeting in the local language shows we know we are the guests; the rest can be worked out together. | | 7 | On the ship. Your cabin steward mentions this is the eighth month away from home. | Keep it brief and polite, because the steward is working. | Leave a larger tip at the end instead of talking. | Ask about their family, learn their name, and use it. | C | Curiosity | The crew are travelers too, far from home for months; a name and a question say we see them as people, not service. | | 8 | Day 5, Istanbul. You arrive at the Grand Bazaar on Sunday and find it closed. | Complain that a tourist site should not close. | Accept it as the merchants' day off, and plan the bazaar for an open day. | Ask the hotel to find a way in. | B | Patience | The bazaar is a working market whose people need a day off; the closure is in the guide, so the fix is planning. | **Provenance:** All eight situations are illustrative, written for this chapter. The Grand Bazaar's Sunday closing and Friday as the main day of congregational prayer come from the trip itinerary in the trip description. The six principles come from the section "The Thoughtful Traveler." **Rules:** Exactly one best response per situation. The position of the best response is fixed as listed (it varies across A, B and C). A situation counts as correct only on the learner's first choice. There are no partial credits. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner reads the situation and the three responses, with the six principles visible. 2. The learner chooses one response. The choice is locked, the best response is marked, and the Principle and Why text appear. 3. The learner moves to the next situation, until all eight are done. 4. At the end, the learner sees a summary: each situation with the principle that decided it, the learner's choices marked right or wrong, and a count of how many times each principle appeared. 5. The learner should notice that every principle decides at least one situation, and that the tempting wrong answers are usually polite-sounding ways of avoiding contact. **Feedback:** Eight situations in fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Good judgment. Principle: ." plus the Why text. Incorrect: "A thoughtful traveler would choose . Principle: ." plus the Why text. The best response is shown after every choice. A running score "Best choices: n of 8" is shown. At the end: "7 or more: you are ready to travel thoughtfully" or "Fewer than 7: reread the six principles and try again." A Restart button clears all answers and the score. **Starting State:** Situation 1 with its three responses, the six principles listed, and the prompt "Which response best fits a thoughtful traveler?" **Chapter Anchors:** Six principles named exactly Curiosity, Humility, Consent, Reciprocity, Patience, Many stories. Eight situations. The Day 8 waiter and the cabin steward appear in the section "Empathy in Travel." The Grand Bazaar is closed on Sundays (Day 5).
